Functions.summary: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. This chapter covers domain and range, combining functions, undoing them with inverses, and modulus graphs. It is the language for most of Add Maths.

body: **Domain**: the set of inputs you are allowed to use. **Range**: the set of outputs you actually get.
**One-one**: each output comes from only one input, e.g. f(x) = 2x + 1.
**Many-one**: two or more inputs give the same output, e.g. f(x) = x², since f(3) = f(−3) = 9.
Only a one-one function has an inverse. If a function is many-one, you can restrict its domain (e.g. x ≥ 0) to make it one-one.
fg(x) means f(g(x)): do **g first**, then f.
Order matters. Usually fg(x) ≠ gf(x).
f²(x) means ff(x), i.e. apply f twice.
For gf to exist, the range of f must fit inside the domain of g.
To find f^{−1}: write y = f(x), make x the subject, then swap x and y.
The domain of f^{−1} is the range of f, and the range of f^{−1} is the domain of f.
The graph of y = f^{−1}(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.
Check: ff^{−1}(x) = x.
|a| is the size of a without its sign: |−4| = 4.
To sketch y = |f(x)|, first sketch y = f(x). Then reflect every part **below** the x-axis up into the x-axis. Parts above stay where they are.
y = |f(x)| is never negative, so its range starts at 0 or above.

examples.q: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x², for x ∈ ℝ. Find fg(2) and gf(x), then solve gf(x) = 25.

steps: Collect the x terms: yx − 3x = −1 − 2y, so x(y − 3) = −(1 + 2y).

examples.q: f(x) = e^{2x} + 1, x ∈ ℝ. State the range of f and find f^{−1}(x), giving its domain.
steps: e^{2x} > 0 for every x, so e^{2x} + 1 > 1. The range is f(x) > 1.
Let y = e^{2x} + 1, so e^{2x} = y − 1.
Take ln of both sides: 2x = ln(y − 1), so x = ½ ln(y − 1).
Swap letters: f^{−1}(x) = ½ ln(x − 1). Its domain is the range of f: x > 1.
examples.answer: Range f(x) > 1; f^{−1}(x) = ½ ln(x − 1), x > 1

practice.q: f(x) = x² + 2, x ≥ 0. State the range of f.
f(x) = 4x − 1 and g(x) = 3/x, x ≠ 0. Find gf(1) and fg(x).
Explain why f(x) = x², x ∈ ℝ, has no inverse.
practice.a: It is many-one, e.g. f(2) = f(−2) = 4, so an output does not lead back to one input.

practice.q: f(x) = ln(x + 3), x > −3. Find f^{−1}(x) and its domain.
Sketch y = |2x − 6| and state where it meets the axes.
practice.a: A V-shape with its vertex at (3, 0), meeting the y-axis at (0, 6).

Functions.tip: fg(x) means g first, then f. Students often do them the wrong way round. Also give a domain for every inverse you write.

Quadratic functions.summary: Quadratics are functions like ax² + bx + c. This chapter uses completing the square to find the turning point, and the discriminant to count roots and to decide whether a line meets a curve. It also covers quadratic inequalities.

body: Write ax² + bx + c as a(x + p)² + q.
If a > 0 the curve is a U-shape with **minimum** value q at x = −p. If a < 0 it is an ∩-shape with **maximum** value q.
The vertex is (−p, q). This gives the range: for a > 0, f(x) ≥ q.
Take a out as a factor first if a ≠ 1.
For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant is b² − 4ac.
b² − 4ac > 0: two different real roots. b² − 4ac = 0: two equal roots. b² − 4ac < 0: no real roots.
Line and curve: substitute the line into the curve to get one quadratic. Then > 0 means the line **cuts** the curve twice, = 0 means it is a **tangent**, and < 0 means it **does not meet** the curve.
Move everything to one side, factorise and find the critical values.
Sketch the parabola. For a U-shape, '> 0' means the outer parts (x < smaller root or x > larger root) and '< 0' means the part in between.
Write the answer properly: −3 < x < 4 for one interval, or x < −3, x > 4 for two separate parts.

examples.q: Write f(x) = 2x² − 12x + 23 in the form a(x + p)² + q. Hence state the minimum value of f and the range of f.
steps: (x − 3)² ≥ 0, so the minimum value is 5, when x = 3.
examples.answer: f(x) = 2(x − 3)² + 5; minimum value 5 at x = 3; range f(x) ≥ 5

examples.q: Find the values of k for which the line y = kx − 1 is a tangent to the curve y = x² + 3.
steps: Rearrange to get one quadratic: x² − kx + 4 = 0.
Check k = 4: x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)² = 0, a repeated root ✓.
The critical values are x = 4 and x = −3.
The curve is a U-shape, so it is above the x-axis outside the roots.
Test x = 0: −12 > 0 is false, which confirms the middle part is excluded.

practice.q: Write 3 + 4x − x² in the form a − (x − b)² and state its maximum value.
Find k if x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two equal roots.
Find the values of m for which x² + 4x + m = 0 has no real roots.
Find the values of c for which the line y = 2x + c does not meet the curve y = x².
practice.a: x² − 2x − c = 0 has discriminant 4 + 4c < 0, so c < −1

practice.q: Solve x² − 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square. Leave surds in your answer.

Quadratic functions.tip: For line-and-curve questions, substitute first and get everything on one side (= 0) before you use b² − 4ac. Many marks are lost on sign errors at this step.

Differentiation.summary: Differentiation gives the gradient of a curve at any point. With it you can find tangents and normals, locate maximum and minimum points, and link rates of change in real situations.

sections.h: Standard results and the chain rule
body: Differentiate each term separately. Constants multiply through and a constant term on its own gives 0.
**Chain rule**: for a function of a function, differentiate the outside, keep the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
For sin, cos and tan, angles must be in **radians**.
formulas: d/dx (sin x) = cos x, d/dx (cos x) = −sin x, d/dx (tan x) = sec² x

body: Use the **product rule** when two functions of x are multiplied, e.g. x² e^{3x}.
Use the **quotient rule** when one function of x is divided by another, e.g. (2x + 1)/(x − 3).
Simplify by taking out common factors at the end.
The gradient of the **tangent** at x = a is the value of dy/dx at a. The **normal** is perpendicular to it, so its gradient is −1/m.
**Stationary points** are where dy/dx = 0.
Second derivative test: d²y/dx² > 0 gives a minimum and d²y/dx² < 0 gives a maximum. You can also check the sign of dy/dx on each side.
In practical problems, write the quantity in one variable, differentiate, set it equal to 0, and show it is a maximum or minimum.

sections.h: Rates of change and small increments
body: **Connected rates**: use the chain rule, e.g. dA/dt = dA/dr × dr/dt.
**Small increments**: δy ≈ (dy/dx) × δx, for a small change δx.
Always include units, e.g. cm² s^{−1}.

steps: u = 2x + 1, so du/dx = 2. v = x − 3, so dv/dx = 1.

examples.q: Find the stationary points of y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 and determine their nature.
steps: d²y/dx² = 6x − 12. At x = 1 it is −6 < 0, so maximum. At x = 3 it is 6 > 0, so minimum.

examples.q: The radius of a circular ink spot grows at 0.5 cm s^{−1}. Find the rate at which its area is increasing when the radius is 4 cm.
steps: Chain rule: dA/dt = dA/dr × dr/dt = 2πr × 0.5 = πr.

practice.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y = e^{2x} + 3 at the point where x = 0.
y = x³. Use differentiation to estimate the change in y when x increases from 2 to 2.01.
A rectangle has perimeter 20 cm. Find its maximum possible area.
practice.a: Sides x and 10 − x, A = 10x − x², dA/dx = 10 − 2x = 0 gives x = 5, d²A/dx² = −2 < 0, so the maximum area is 25 cm²

Differentiation.tip: When asked for the 'nature' of a stationary point, show the second derivative value (or the sign change) and state the conclusion. Writing just 'maximum' without justification loses the mark.
